Nour had not lost an argument in the debate seminar all term. Yuki, who taught it, watched him take apart classmates' points with a grin, and she had noticed other things too. He had spent a week arguing with his landlord over a small deposit charge and won, then lost the room when the landlord refused to renew. He had stayed up until dawn winning an online quarrel and slept through a presentation.
After class Yuki asked, "Which argument this term was worth the most to you?" Nour started to answer, then stopped. "The landlord one, I guess," he said, and laughed, but not as loudly. Yuki did not say anything else. She packed her bag and told him the seminar hall was hers until five if he wanted to talk.

qa.q: What did Nour win against his landlord, and what did it cost him?
qa.a: He won an argument over a small deposit charge, but the landlord then refused to renew his room.

qa.q: What is Nour feeling when he stops and laughs less loudly at Yuki's question?
qa.a: He seems unsure and a little uncomfortable, perhaps beginning to doubt that his wins were worth what they cost.

qa.q: What does Yuki do that leaves room for Nour to reflect?
qa.a: She asks a question and does not lecture, then leaves the hall open for a conversation if he wants one.

qa.q: How might Nour's classmates see his winning streak?
qa.a: They may admire his skill but also feel steamrolled. Nour's constant winning may make it harder for them to enjoy discussing things with him.

grounding: A teacher sees a brilliant student win arguments but make poor life choices, and asks a question about what is worth pursuing.

Yamini had taught literature at the women's college for eleven years, and Ira was the sharpest student she had met in a long time. In class, Ira dismantled every argument, even Yamini's own. In the hostel she led a two-month campaign against a timetable change and won it, and the notice board proudly carried her name.
But Yamini also knew that Ira had quietly dropped her place in the poetry society, the one thing she had said she loved, to keep the campaign going. Her attendance had slipped. Her essays, once careful, had turned into clever tricks with words.
In the staffroom, Yamini said to a colleague, "She can win anything. I don't know if she's asked what for." Then she wrote Ira's name on a slip and put it on top of her tea cup, to remind herself to invite her for a chat.

qa.q: How many years had Yamini taught literature at the college?
qa.a: She had taught there for eleven years.

qa.q: What is Yamini worried about when she says she doesn't know if Ira has asked what for?
qa.a: She is worried that Ira's cleverness is being spent on wins that cost her the things she loves, such as the poetry society.

qa.q: What small step could Yamini take in the chat she plans?
qa.a: She could ask Ira what she got out of the campaign and what she missed, and listen. She should not lecture her about her choices.

qa.q: What might Ira be feeling about leaving the poetry society?
qa.a: Ira may be feeling torn or guilty. She said she loved poetry, but the pull of the campaign may have felt more urgent, and she may not have noticed the price.

grounding: A teacher sees a brilliant student win arguments while making costly life choices; cleverness handles problems but wisdom weighs what is worth it.

Dear Disha,

I've coached debate for eleven years, and you are the sharpest speaker I've had. When you took apart the other team's economic case in the finals, the judges stopped writing.

That is why I'm writing. This year you won every argument and, I think, lost a few things that mattered more. You argued your way out of the lab project and left Rhea to finish it alone. You told me the scholarship interview was "beneath" you because they asked a lazy question. You haven't come to practice since the finals, and I miss you there.

Being clever tells you how to win a point. It doesn't tell you which points are worth winning.

My door is open on Tuesdays, if you want to talk it through.

Lokesh

qa.q: How many years has Lokesh coached debate?
qa.a: Eleven years.

qa.q: What does the letter suggest Lokesh feels about Disha?
qa.a: Lokesh admires Disha's sharpness but is worried and a little sad that this cleverness is leading to choices that cost a lab partner and an opportunity.

qa.q: What would you advise Disha after reading the letter?
qa.a: Disha could take up the Tuesday offer, and ask before the next fight whether winning it is worth what might be lost.

qa.q: How might Rhea have felt about the lab project?
qa.a: Rhea was left to finish it alone, so Rhea probably felt let down and used after Disha argued out of the work.

grounding: Shows a coach noticing that a brilliant student wins arguments but makes poor choices about what is worth pursuing.

"You want to hear about the one who taught me the most? I'm Damini, and I've been a maths tutor in Bhopal for nine years. His name was Vikas.
He was nineteen and faster than me. Genuinely. He'd find the flaw in any proof I put on the board, and he'd argue with his parents the same way. He argued his way out of engineering, then out of the design course, then out of the job his uncle offered. Every time, he had a perfect case.
Last winter I met him at the bus stand. He was working nights at a call centre, tired, still arguing, this time with the bus conductor about change.
I used to think if you're clever enough, life sorts itself. Vikas taught me that being able to win every debate is not the same as knowing what's worth fighting for."

qa.q: Where did Damini meet Vikas last winter?
qa.a: At the bus stand.

qa.q: What does Damini seem to feel on recalling the meeting with Vikas at the bus stand?
qa.a: Damini seems saddened and a little regretful, seeing that the brilliant student who could win every argument ended up tired and stuck.

qa.q: What could a tutor like Damini try with a student like Vikas?
qa.a: Instead of only admiring the arguments, the tutor could ask questions like 'What do you want in five years, and does this choice help?'

qa.q: What might Vikas's parents have experienced during his teenage years?
qa.a: They probably felt frustrated and worn out, losing every argument while watching him drop course after course.

grounding: Shows a tutor observing a brilliant student who wins every argument yet keeps making poor life choices.

I run the physics lab in the second-year block, so I see everyone. Tushar stands out. When Professor Sen made an error in a derivation, Tushar caught it and defended his correction for twenty minutes until the professor gave up. The class clapped.
But I also see the attendance register. He's missed half the practicals this term because he "already knows the results." Last week he argued with the canteen staff that his late fee was illegal and won, then missed the viva.
I don't know what's going on inside him. Maybe he's bored. Maybe something at home. He always has an answer when I ask, and it's always a clever one.
Yesterday he left his lab file on the bench. It was empty after page three. I kept it, and I'll hand it back tomorrow and ask how I can help.

qa.q: How many practicals has Tushar missed this term?
qa.a: He has missed half the practicals this term.

qa.q: What does the narrator seem to feel about Tushar, and why?
qa.a: The observer is uncertain what is going on inside Tushar, wondering whether he is bored or something at home is troubling him, and is concerned for him.

qa.q: What small step does the observer plan, and why could it help?
qa.a: Handing back the file and asking how they can help opens a real conversation about his choices instead of another argument.

qa.q: How might Professor Sen see Tushar?
qa.a: The professor probably sees a gifted but exhausting student, impressive at spotting errors but hard to guide toward what actually matters.

grounding: Shows an observer in a lab noticing a clever student who wins arguments yet neglects the work that counts.

September. At the inter-college debate, Vikas took apart the other team's case in four minutes flat, and the hall roared. Sangeeta, who taught his philosophy section, clapped too, though she noticed he had argued the side he'd told her last week he didn't believe.
November. Passing the attendance office, she heard Vikas, quick and charming, talking the clerk into overlooking three weeks of missed labs. He had joined four clubs, quit his internship after a quarrel with his manager, and looked as if he hadn't slept.
February. He stood at her desk holding his results. "Sixty-one percent. I'm sharper than half that class." Sangeeta nodded. "You are. What were you trying to win this year?" He opened his mouth, then closed it.

qa.q: How long did Vikas take to take apart the other team's case?
qa.a: He took four minutes flat.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling as she clapped in September?
qa.a: She was impressed but also uneasy, because he had argued a side he had told her he didn't believe.

qa.q: Why might Sangeeta's question help Vikas more than praise or a lecture?
qa.a: It makes him weigh what was worth pursuing this year and at what cost, which his quick arguing had skipped.

qa.q: What is it like for Vikas when he cannot answer her question?
qa.a: He probably feels stung and confused, since being sharp has always been enough and, for once, it is not.

grounding: Shows a teacher watching a brilliant student win every argument while his choices go badly, separating cleverness from wisdom.
